utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I apologise. Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances for today's Status Conference, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This morning for the Prosecution, in order to match the Defence, it's Joanna Korner, Matthew Olmsted, and Alex Demirdjian, assisted by Case Manager Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic appearing for the Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Aleksandar Aleksic, Igor Pantelic, and Miroslav Cuskic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. The -- you would all have received from the Senior Liaison Officer an agenda for today's exercise, and the -- I'm reminding myself as to what this contains, and incorporating the latest information that we have on Witness 008, and in -- in that -- in the context of the item listed as -- at A, in what order will the OTP call its remaining witnesses after the recess, included in that is the current position on witness number 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Does Your Honour wish to go straight to that rather than the first two? The first two, although they're in italics for some reason, but I'm perfectly happy to deal with that -- that question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, you may proceed as you prefer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, no, Your Honours, I mean, I'm perfectly happy to deal with that, because it's obviously the last remaining bits of the Prosecution case. Witness 008, as Your Honours know and the Defence know, has been in hospital for roughly the last two weeks. The report that we received from VWS the day before yesterday, which, I understand from Mr. Krgovic, last night obviously the Defence weren't informed of this - and I see Mr. Zecevic shaking his head - he was not fit enough to give evidence or, indeed, in the view of the hospital, should not remain another night in The Hague. He's been returned to where he lives for further medical treatment, and that took place yesterday morning. And VWS sent a memo through to some of the parties anyhow. What we're seeking to do is to see if we can arrange a videolink after the new year. He would be the last witness. The order of witnesses will be the two witnesses Your Honours have ordered to be re-called for further cross-examination on Monday, the 10th, which is, I think, 181 and 191, in either order; followed by Witness 228; followed by Ewan Brown. And because of the shortened week, we anticipate that Mr. Brown will go into the following Monday, maybe Tuesday. We anticipate he'd start on the Tuesday after -- the Tuesday, the 11th. And I believe we're sitting a few hours on Wednesday; I can't now remember. So we've got an extended sitting on Tuesday, we'll sit on the Wednesday, certainly he'll be completed in-chief during that time. And then cross-examination the following Monday. And then, finally, Witness 008. And that will conclude the Prosecution's case at present. I'm -- I was slightly wondering what the question was meant to imply, "How long will the OTP need after outstanding decisions are rendered in order to close its case." But maybe we can come onto that -- well, in fact, I suppose that's the next witness. Your Honours, I don't quite understand that question. I have to tell you. It's how long is a piece of string. I don't know what Your Honours' rulings are going to be. If Your Honours rule against us on the exhumations, then we'll have to call all the exhumation evidence; that will take some organising and presumably take a little time. The quater witnesses, which Your Honours still have to rule on. If Your Honours rule against us on that, we'll have to look for other witnesses. But, as I say, at the present, I'm not quite clear what Your Honour means -- what Your Honours mean by that question, B. Because we would close our case, subject to the rulings, immediately after Witness 008.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry. If I might interrupt to go back to the item listed at 1, the -- I -- you may not find what I'm about to say helpful, but from the Chamber's point of view, we're stating the obvious when we say that the -- we are not unaware of the necessity which has become critical of disposing of the outstanding motions before the Prosecution closes its case, and against the boundaries in terms of dates that we have indicated by which we expect the Prosecution's case to have been completed, that means, internally for us, the deadline against which we are working to ensure that all of the outstanding motions are dealt with. As I said, you may not find that sufficiently, precisely, helpful, and -- but that's where we are.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. We would -- we had some hopes that -- we know the Defence, as Your Honours have seen from the e-mail that was sent, have a particular interest in the Rules ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- to add a layer of confusion or uncertainty to what I have just said, one of the things that is operating in the mind of the Trial Chamber is that the -- after the decisions would have been rendered, the -- we -- we must accept that the parties may contemplate the matter of -- of -- of an appeal. And that is -- it is against that background that the -- we think that there would be a seven-day buffer after the decisions are rendered.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we understand that. We were hoping that we would get some decisions by the end of this week. May I say that our list of decisions which have never been ruled on, save for one of them, which was the one in February of this year, for leave to amend its 65 ter -- sorry. Yes, for leave to amend its 65 ter exhibit list to add the documents which have been marked for identification which we'd filed in February of this year, and Your Honours may recall I've mentioned it from time to time because we still have to file a further one to deal with subsequent documents which have been marked for identification, and the Defence, likewise, I think, Your Honours have been told, are going to file a similar one in respect of their documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, I could say that there is a decision on MFI documents which should be out today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Well, that would be very -- Your Honours, may I say that will be extremely helpful, because all we were about to suggest was our list doesn't include where Your Honours have written -- sorry, issued an oral decision that says "written reasons to follow." We noticed one came out yesterday. Can we say - we hope in the spirit of helpfulness - we've accepted the oral rulings. Obviously at some stage reasons would be useful. But it doesn't seem to me that that's the most urgent thing to deal with. What we really need is ones that have never been ruled on at all. And we -- and I'm grateful for Your Honours indicating we'll get the MFI decision today. As I was about to say, the other one that seems to be, and obviously is, of some importance to the Defence is the one that was filed in May of last year -- sorry, yes, May of last year, relating to Rule 66(C). So, Your Honours, we would hope that we would get the decisions by the time we call our last witness. As far as -- which could lead me on to item number 2, the joint Defence request to extend the time to reply to the bar table motion. We think that's a matter for Your Honours. I mean, Your Honours now have the timetable in mind of what you want to do. So we take a neutral position on this. If they get their 35 days, that brings us to January the 6th, from the date we filed the motion, which was December the 2nd, and that -- if we were given seven days to respond, that takes us up to the 13th of January. So -- but, as I say, we think that's entirely a matter for Your Honours. So we're neutral. Your Honours, I think the next set of questions is really for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Item 3(c).

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, in order to be able to give the proper answer to the question posed as 3(c), we would obviously need to know the whole parameter of the case. Before that, I'm afraid we cannot be very helpful to Your Honours. We are, at the moment, analysing the Prosecutor's case. But before we know the decisions, so we have the full decisions, the full body of decisions which are pending, and before we hear the rest of the -- the Office of the Prosecutor case, we will not be able to indicate whether we are going to trigger the 98 bis submission or not. Your Honours, the -- you -- are you certainly aware of the fact that during the case, during the case, during the Prosecutor's case, we had additional, I believe, 57 new witnesses which were added in the meantime, in the course of the case. Your Honours, let me remind you that the last batch before the -- before we started, the trial was 79, and now we reached 165, which means that the disclosure more than doubled during -- in the course of the trial. Therefore, we do have to analyse that from the perspective of the whole parameter of the case. Therefore, we need all the decisions and to hear all the evidence which the Office of the Prosecutor intends to call in its case before we can -- we can -- we can be able to assist the Trial Chamber whether we are going to trigger the 98 bis or not. What I can -- what I can say at this point is that after the rulings, after the rulings of the Trial Chamber, we will be able within the 24 hours to inform the Trial Chamber whether we are going to trigger the 98 bis. And also, if we are triggering the 98 bis, we can start on Monday after the end of the Prosecutor's case, which I would say is the 24th of -- of the January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, I think those last two answers are helpful, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Because the -- I appreciate that any position that you would have had to the question in its stark form would be tentative. And dependant on the -- whatever your -- having regard to the stage that we're at, whatever your -- wherever you thought you were tending to be, that would have to abide the completion of the Prosecution's case and all its aspects. But I understand from your last two answers that you would not need a great deal of time, once the Prosecution were to draw a line under its case, for you to indicate finally, what your position is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours. So immediately after we have the rulings, the whole set of rulings by the Trial Chamber, within 24 hours we will inform the Trial Chamber of our intention to trigger 98 bis. And if we -- if we decide to trigger the 98 bis submission, then we can start on Monday after the close of the Prosecutor's case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, do you diverge from Mr. Zecevic on this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was joint submission by Mr. Zecevic so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I have to say I do not see how the re-call of two witnesses for further cross-examination, the evidence of Mr. Brown, and any rulings on -- on -- that Your Honours make will really alter the position as it is today. We have called 98.8 per cent of the evidence we intend to call. The rulings which await - you may think, if you consider the matter - really don't affect it. And I think Mr. Zecevic should be in a position, and Mr. Krgovic, to be slightly more helpful than they have been today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We might agree entirely with everything you have just said, Ms. Korner, but I -- I don't know that we could press counsel for a more definitive answer than they have given today. Indeed, I would presume to add that -- I'm somewhat surprised that they haven't been able to volunteer and give us some inkling as to where they are, but more than that I wouldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, it's clear, Your Honour -- well, all right. I've made the position. If Your Honour don't feel that it would be right to press the Defence further, then I can't really urge Your Honours to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: At the risk of -- no, I ... I -- I wouldn't say what I was about to say in -- in fairness to Defence counsel, suggesting that the answer to (d) may very much reflect what the answer was to (c). So I didn't say that. But could we have a response the item listed at item 3(d)?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Your Honours, as you quite correctly stated, depending on the -- on the decision of 98 bis, the Defence informed the Trial Chamber already in March of this year, during the Status Conference held on the 19th of March, that we would need, in case we are to present the Defence case, that we would need two months to prepare the Defence case. Which means that in -- in -- in period of 60 days after the decision on 98 bis, on the 60th day we will file the 65 ter list for the Defence case, and that is all the information that I think I can give to the Trial Chamber at this point. However, in order to -- to be as fair as possible, I have discussed with Mr. Krgovic, and if we are presenting the Defence cases, of course, based on the -- the 98 bis decision, we will be able to finish - and we can assure the Trial Chamber - that the both Defences will finish the Defence case before the winter break next year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We -- we -- we recall, Mr. Zecevic, your indication that you would require two months. But could you, for the record, assist us as to why - having regard to the progress of this trial, and that the -- in the nature of trials, the Defence case doesn't -- whereas it probably only finally coalesces at that the close of the case for the Prosecution, but nevertheless it is constantly being formed from the -- from even before the trial begins - why you would require as long as two months?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we are to present a Defence case, we want to be as specific as we can. That requires us to analyse the Office of the Prosecutor case in its entirety. As I stated before, we had 57 witnesses which have not been even considered before the trial. We have more than doubled the disclosure, which had not been considered before the trial. This obviously has changed the -- the Office of the Prosecutor's case immensely, I must say, and, therefore, all our preparation in the pre-trial phase for our Defence case has been in some way -- has to be in some way altered. Your Honours, we need the time to talk to the -- to the witnesses, have -- have their witness statements prepared in order to shorten the -- the time needed for the presentation of the Defence case. We need to finalize the -- the expert reports. And we have to select documents which we are going to be relying upon in the Defence case. And I stated already in March, Your Honours, that we would need two months, 60 days, for that. And I'm afraid I can't be of any more help to -- to the Trial Chamber in -- in that regard as -- as I stand here in the -- we haven't altered our position a bit from -- from the -- from the March Status Conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you for your indications. And, of course, we understand that one of the fine arts of life is to make safe predictions of the future. But, if you say that you need a full 60 days before you can present your witness list, then we would need at least a week before we could have the Pre-Trial Conference. And after the Pre-Trial Conference, at least a couple of days would be needed to make whatever adjustments are determined at the Pre-Trial Conference. So what you're saying is that you're not asking for two months; you're effectively asking for two and a half months. Unless what you really mean is that on the 60th day you would be able to call your first witness. But that would then require that you submit your 65 ter list of witnesses and exhibits much earlier, two or three weeks prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is precisely why I stated, Your Honours, very clear on the record this morning that 60 days is the time needed for the preparation of the case. Preparation of the case means before we file our 65 ter list. Because after that, after that, Your Honours, when we file the 65 ter list, when we file -- when we -- when we disclose to the Office of the Prosecutor the 94 bis expert report, when we disclose to the Prosecutor the statements of the witnesses, there's no more preparation for us and all the exhibits. So we are not -- we are not in a position to prepare anymore after -- after we file 65 ter list. Because that is -- that is the parameter that we are offering as -- as a frame of our Defence case. Your Honours, that is why I suggest and I tried to assure the Trial Chamber what -- whatever we are -- we are perfectly aware of the time that is needed for the Trial Chamber and the -- and our friends from the Office of the Prosecutor to analyse our 65 ter list and the time needed for the preparation of the Defence conference, Pre-Defence Conference. But, again, what we are assuring the Trial Chamber is that whatever the date is when we actually start calling our first witness, the Defence, the both Defences will finish by winter break of next year. And I think that -- that -- that's -- that is in complete conformity with the -- with the -- with the schedule of this case as we understand it from -- from the words of Mr. President in his address to the Security Council and the schedule which is available to us, because it says that the Judgement in this case is -- is expected to be in September 2012. That is -- that is our understanding. Therefore, we think that this gives more than enough time for -- for -- for the Trial Chamber to render the Judgement by the time anticipated in this case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. That is a matter which the Chamber will have to consider --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm waiting for Mr. Zecevic -- sorry, for Mr. Krgovic to say anything, but I'd like to say something about what's just been said, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What Mr. Zecevic said is a joint submission by both Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I say this, first of all, Your Honours have sat through this case and have read our pre-trial brief and you would have seen that the nature of our case has not changed in one iota what we have said in respect of how Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Zupljanin are indeed to be held responsible for the crimes alleged. The extra witnesses called, 44 were to cover adjudicated facts, so, Your Honours, that simply dealt with matters that would otherwise have been in evidence as adjudicated facts from other cases. Stanisic surrendered to the Tribunal on the 10th of March -- 11th of March, 2005. That's five years ago. Since which time, which is clear from his interview where he mentioned that he was reserving things for his Defence, he has been preparing his Defence. If the Defence are in a position to say that if they don't start until what would then be effectively some time mid-April and probably after Easter, which is, we have to say, not in the spirit of what the Security Council wants this Tribunal to do. They are in a position to say that they will have finished by Christmas, both of them, well then they know, roughly, what they're going to be dealing with in terms of the Defence case, I'm afraid. And so they've clearly got an idea of what Defence evidence they want to call, even if they haven't finalized it. As Judge Harhoff has pointed out, if we wait until whenever it is in March to get the list, there has to be a gap, first of all, to have the Defence conference, and, secondly, for us to do the researches we're entitled to do on the witnesses. And so, Your Honours, we would submit, particularly in the light of the fact that both Defence teams are well staffed, have had ample time to prepare, that, really, that is too long to wait for the list of witnesses an exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, could you give us an indication about the time you need to -- after having the witness list and the exhibit list?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- sorry. It depends on the number of witnesses that are listed. But, clearly, we have to do our own searches on those witnesses to be in a position to -- to see what it is we want to deal with, with this particular witnesses. We are not in -- we will be reluctant, also, to -- to do what the Defence have been doing, which is, namely, to interview witnesses as they appear, shortly before they testify. We don't think that's at all a satisfactory method of going about things. So we want time to investigate, ourselves. So, give or take, we'd probably be asking for a month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: As I said, this is something that the Chamber will have to come back on. But there is one brief comment I feel constrained to make before we leave this topic, and that is -- and if I misconstrued what Mr. Zecevic intended to convey, I apologise, but it is that the -- such reports as the President is required to make to the Security Council as to the progress of these matters before the Tribunal would reflect what the Tribunal is doing and not the other way around as being the -- this closing date having been indicated and it means that the parties have until that date to do whatever they have to do. So that if, in fact, the Trial Chamber in managing the progress of the matter is able to expedite and speed things, it is its duty to so. So the -- the -- such comments that are made outside of the Chamber, and by which I include the reports to which Mr. Zecevic refers, are not determinative at all of the way in which this matter will be run. In terms of the item listed at 3(e), there is three -- and (f), there is a subsidiary that the Chamber has which Defence counsel may not be able to answer immediately, but we would wish their report on it as soon as possible, and the -- well, the first question is stated is -- as stated in the agenda, is that the -- this trial, involving persons who are jointly accused, we assume that the conventional practice would be followed and that is that the case of the first named accused will be the first to proceed. The ancillary question or subsidiary question - however you choose to characterise it - is that Defence counsel have indicated that there are a number of joint witnesses, and the Chamber would wish to be informed, enlightened, as to how they intend to deal with these joint witnesses, having regard to the fact that we are faced with separate accused. Although they are jointly charged, they are separate cases. So, as I said, we would -- we appreciate that you mightn't be able to answer that subsidiary question at this moment, but are we safe in assuming that it is the case of Stanisic which will proceed first?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, your assuming is right, that the Stanisic case would go first. As you correctly indicated, the ancillary question we cannot, of course, give an answer today to the Trial Chamber, but as soon as practically possible, we will be able to provide that answer to the Trial Chamber. Of course, pending the 98 bis decision. That is -- goes without saying, I guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I should say, and I omitted to say this earlier, that today's exercise is a purely practical one in terms of managing the -- and projecting where we go forward. And to the extent that it may imply that the 98 bis exercise would result in an adverse ruling for the Defence is not something that is in any way suggested. We're taking a purely practical approach as to the -- what would happen if the Defence -- if the accused have to mount a Defence. So no questions that we would have raised today or nothing that we should have said should in any way suggest that we have prejudged any decision that would be taken on any 98 bis application or submissions. The -- as we wrap up this item, I am, again, constrained to inquire of the Defence counsel whether there's any -- whether they where able to indicate the number of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are not able to indicate the number of witnesses, but we anticipate that the -- that the -- as -- as you correctly said, and that is why we say that we assure the Trial Chamber that we can finish by winter recess, is that the number of witnesses will be joint for both -- both accused. And as a matter of fact, I informed already the Trial Chamber that we will have some joint experts in this -- in this respect. So therefore that is why we -- we can give the assurances to the Trial Chamber that we will finish by winter break. And it doesn't mean that we know what it -- what our Defence case is going to be at this point at all, which is contrary to -- to what Ms. Korner said. And I would also like to -- to state one thing: Your Honours, the Office of the Prosecutor indicated first that in seven months they will close their case. Then it was extended until July. And now we are coming to the January next year, probably, for the end of their case. Therefore, any comments on the -- on the length of Defence case or -- or the time required for the preparation of the Defence case, I think, is inappropriate if it comes from the Office of the Prosecutor. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may add something. Three months ago I could have said to you with certainty how many witnesses the Zupljanin Defence will call and what our Defence case would look like. However, in the last three months, in relation to my client, via adjudicated facts, the OTP introduced so many new facts and so many pieces of new evidence that I'm now unable to tell you how many witnesses we would be calling and how many pieces of evidence I would need to tender in order to challenge everything that the Prosecution has stated here in the last three months. This is why I'm unable to tell you now what evidence we would be relying, in relation to which facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. There is a question, moving on, as -- there is a question as to the -- whether the Defence require the investigator Michael Koehler to testify. Could the Prosecution -- is there any light that the Prosecution can shed on this?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, we put that in because together with the bar table motion we have included, in fact, I think somewhat in advance of the new rule, the provenance of the documents we seek to put in. Mr. Koehler made a statement saying that he had dealt with that column, checked the entries on the relevant forms to show whether the witnesses came -- the witnesses -- the documents, plus a number of other matters. Now, Your Honours, we thought it right to inquire whether the Defence wished to cross-examine on other matters that he's dealt with which are contained in his statement. He gives a list of the various activities he's undertaken and/or in respect of any of the documents for which he has given the provenance, and that's the reason we put that in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, as we indicated in our motion for extension, we are still analysing the bar table document. But as it stands at this -- at this point, we don't think that we would require Mr. Koehler to testify. That is on behalf of Stanisic Defence, because I haven't consulted with this with Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. The query that the OTP has about the status of the site visit material, we are somewhat at a loss as to what the -- their -- the query is about. Because we thought it was well settled that the evidence is not received at a site visit, and the protocols about the site visits, which would have been stated at the beginning -- and we would have had occasion -- there's one occasion that I distinctly remember - there may be more than one - where, in terms of a specific photograph, when it had been submitted, and the Chamber was satisfied that it was entirely new and that the usual rules about relevance and absence of prejudice would not have -- would have meant that no harm was done to the case of either accused by admitting it, that we took the exceptional decision to allow that in. But the basic rule is that material garnered on the occasion of the site visit is inadmissible. So could the Prosecution indicate what their concerns is here or what their interest is here? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it came up for two reasons. The first is this: That it is not clear from the protocol of the site visit, which I may say was not something that existed when we carried out a site visit in Brdjanin, where everything was recorded, that none of it will be used in evidence, because under the protocol, which Mr. Smith kindly turned up for me, four reads: The photographs may be admitted into evidence at a later stage. And then if any -- 5: If any specific observations are made, these will be recorded using an audio recorder. This recording will be transcribed upon the return of the Trial Chamber. The transcript may be admitted into evidence at a later stage. And that's all very up in the air, as it is -- as it were, and so we're anxious to know: Is Your Honours' final decision on this that none of the evidence, photographs, or whatever, except for the exception you made, or the transcripts of the recorded conversations will come into evidence? That's the first matter. The second matter that arises is this: If Your Honours, as a result of Your Honours' own observations, have queries about evidence they've heard, about places or incidents, because of those observations, then rather than, as it were, appearing in the Judgement, if Your Honours have any matters that they have queries about, they ought to be raised with counsel. I don't know whether Your Honours do have such queries; but if do, then can we simply suggest this: That if there are matters that you find in some way raise questions about the evidence you've heard in the court, well, then, we would suggest that the way of dealing with it is to raise those matters with counsel so that we can deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, I would have thought that goes without saying, Ms. Korner. And that the Chamber could not substitute its own observations for evidence. And to the extent that there appeared -- that -- that any Judge's observation appeared to be inconsistent or conflicted with the evidence, then it's a matter that -- that the Chamber would be bound, as a matter of principle, to raise with counsel and in the extreme case to have a witness called by -- called by the Bench itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I'm grateful for that. I mean, I imagined that was the position, but I thought it ought to be clear on the record. And equally - I think Your Honours made that clear now - although the protocol says "may," Your Honours are ruling that it will not come into any or be used as any evidence at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Personally, Ms. Korner, I am always reluctant to use the word "never." To repeat what we have done so far, is that when it has been shown in specific instances that it should be admitted, we have done so; and, no doubt, it is unlikely to happen in the remainder of the Prosecution's case. But as the Defence case develops, the similar applications may arise. But in each case, the decision to admit this new evidence is an exception to the general rule, as to matters that were thrown up by the site visit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I fully understand. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: As for the decision included in point (e) on the agenda, which is the decision on the motion on Rule 66(C), we had hoped that we could issue today an oral ruling which would indicate the disposition of that decision, but I am afraid that, simply, the final disposition has not been brushed up to such an extent that I dare issue that oral ruling now without running into difficulties when I finally get to the point where I can finalize the disposition. But one thing that I can assure you is that it will be issued first thing in the new year and certainly before your last witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, can I say, I think that is more Mr. Krgovic. The Prosecution don't -- don't have a vested interest in that one so much. It doesn't affect their case one way or another. But I think Mr. Krgovic is the one who wants that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence of Stojan Zupljanin is particularly interested in resolving this issue, and we would ask that the ruling be handed down, if possible, before the end of the Prosecution case so that the Defence would have enough time to go over these documents before the Defence case starts. And since the Trial Chamber indicated that the ruling would be handed down before the end of the year, that would mean that we would have enough time to go over the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. That stands as indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. The items listed at (f) and (g), these were included on the agenda by the Defence, and it would be helpful if counsel could expand on what we have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Your Honours, before we go to -- to (f) and (g), and (h), I guess, I would just like to clarify the -- the -- the item under letter (d). It is my understanding that -- of your -- of Your Honours that we -- that the MFI decision will be issued shortly. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then I guess the -- the letter (d) is moot for the moment. Your Honours ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, concerning the -- the -- the item under letter (f), you will remember that I made a submission, an observation, actually, to the Trial Chamber about the late disclosure of the -- of the batch of Doboj documents. What -- what we -- we are in a communication with our friends from the Office of the Prosecutor. What we are suggesting is two alternative approaches. One is we gave a list of the documents that we think are relevant and -- and are proposing that this list of document, these documents, be admitted on agreement base into the evidence. On agreement of the parties. If that would not be acceptable for the Office of the Prosecutor, then -- then we suggested that maybe the other way would be that we re-call the witness, or some of the witnesses, from Doboj, the OTP witnesses who testified over here, in the course of Defence case. But for that we would obviously need the assistance of the Office of the Prosecutor. And those are the two alternatives that we have in order to be able to expedite the proceedings in this case as much as we can and to be of assistance to the Trial Chamber in that respect. That is concerning letter (f). As to issue of -- under letter (g), status of disclosure of the Pecanac documents, we received yesterday a list of -- or, actually, a disclosure of 23 documents which the Office of the Prosecutor feels might be relevant for this case, and -- and I'm pretty sure, because we asked that we be disclosed the whole list of the Pecanac documents, that we will be receiving that shortly and that, therefore, there would be, I hope, no -- no -- no need for the Trial Chamber to be involved in -- in this disclosure, because I -- I'm pretty sure that we -- the parties will be able to deal with this on the -- on the direct basis. And as for (h), the exhumation database status, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I might speak to that, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That is a matter which could be looked at from two ways. One way of looking at it is that it is an extremely simply and straightforward matter. However, looked at from another perspective, it is exceedingly complicated, having a variety of layers of issues which are not readily reconciled with each other; let me put it that way. And it is the -- the Chamber is acutely aware of the need to dispose of this in some manner or other as -- as soon as possible, but the consideration of the several issues has, quite frankly, bedevilled us as to what the eventual disposition would be. The only thing that we can say is that we know we have to make a decision; that's our job. And we had anticipated - I should say we had hoped - that we would have been able to dispose of that that this week. But obviously that is not now going to happen. But it is something which we are very actively considering, and we -- we -- we hope that in the first week after we resume that we will be able to -- to give a decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Could I just ask a question in extension of the Presiding Judge's comment. One thing that is not completely clear - at least to me - is the time when the Defence teams were, in fact, given access to the database and to the source documents. Because I would have thought that during the negotiations that took place between the Prosecution and the two Defence teams since June, that the Defence teams would have had access to the database and the source documents and that, in effect, several attempts were made during those months, that is to say, during July, August, and September, to try it out. But when I read your submissions, it seems as if this was not the case. So I'm just wondering if it is true that you did not have access to the database and the source documents until, I think, sometime in October; and why was that? Are you able to clarify?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if I may -- if I may inform the Trial Chamber, I will try to be as precise as I can, because I don't have the precise dates. As far as I recall, the -- the first document was the motion filed by the -- by the Office of the Prosecutor on the 22nd of July. I think July. Just immediately before -- immediately before the -- the -- the break, the summer break. In the course of that week, we had some -- some discussion with the Office of the Prosecutor, and it was -- it was presented to us that we will be receiving that in order that we see the database documents, the spreadsheets, and if we can give a comment, which we agreed to, but then the Office of the Prosecutor filed the motion immediately to the Trial Chamber. Therefore, there was no point of negotiating -- there was no negotiations prior to the -- to the document being filed in the -- on -- by the motion on the 22nd of July. After we reviewed the documents, we found that there is one -- almost 1800 names which do not appear in the schedules, and then we went for the -- to the meeting with the -- with the Office of the Prosecutor, where we opposed that, and that is the first submission that Ms. Korner and myself made to the Trial Chamber as to the legal question whether or not this would be allowed or is -- or is allowed or not. At that point, on that meeting, which was in September, we requested the disclosure of all the underlying material concerning only the victims listed in the schedules to the indictment, because that is our position. And that list, that -- these underlying documents were disclosed to us on the 24th -- 19th of October. And that is when -- that is the first time we saw the underlying documents, on the 19th of October this year. We reviewed that underlying documents and then I made a submission stating that we cannot accept or cannot agree on the -- on the spreadsheet offered by the Office of the Prosecutor because the underlying documents are not existing. In our opinion. And that is -- that is the situation, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: May I, just to clarify, ask this: What you -- what was disclosed to you in the beginning with the motion is the spreadsheets A and B?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Only.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Then in October you got the underlying documents for the witnesses listed in the indictment; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: For victims. Victims listed in the -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Victims listed in the indictment. Oh, I said witness, sorry. Victims listed in the indictment. Of course. In what form did you get those documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, again, Your Honours, we got the spreadsheet with the hyperlinks, with the hyperlinks to the alleged underlying documents which would be proving the data indicated in the spreadsheets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So we again received, I believe, four spreadsheets or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- even more, and some documents to that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: To fully understand this - and I'm addressing the Prosecution as well - there are the spreadsheets, the original spreadsheets. I understand how you got the underlying documents. Now my question is: Is that -- is that part of the database? Is that the database we're talking about? Or is the database still something else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And -- and could I, because now I'm confused, could I put another question to -- in extension of Judge Delvoie's question, namely: When you received the first spreadsheets in July, were those spreadsheets hyperlinked?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. No, Your Honours. Those are just the annexes to the motion filed by the Office of the Prosecutor on 22nd July, Annex A and Annex B, just a list of the victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: List of victims plus the list of the documents without hyperlinks. In Annex B had you a list of the documents, if I understand it well. Isn't that right? The list of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have it over here, Your Honours. If you just bear with me one second, I will check. Your Honours, I have over here the both -- the both documents. The annexes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I have B in front of me on the screen. I have the Annex B on the screen. Annex A as well. But Annex B gives names of victims. And then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And then some data --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- but not the documents proving that they -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... no, no, not the documents itself. But it gives -- it gives the numbers of the -- the title and the numbers of the documents. But without hyperlink.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I explain that the hyperlinking -- that there was a delay, because we handed over all that. Then the Defence said it would be much simpler if we could hyperlink it for them so they could actually see it. Then that took forever. But it was at their request. They didn't want to go and hunt around, using the ERNs, and I understand that perfectly. But they asked to us to do that and so we did it. And it was a major, major effort. But can I say, Your Honours, straight away, from virtually day one of this case, or the first 65 ter, we have been saying we were prepared to let the Defence inspect anything they wanted to in respect of exhumations. I believe it was when Judge Harhoff was the Pre-Trial Judge. And he may recall -- I forgot what -- 65 ter, we said, We are hoping the exhumations will be agreed. There is a database. The Defence can inspect at any stage at which they wish to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, before we go into all that. In order to understand precisely what is available and what is not available, when you're mentioning a database, what do you mean by a database?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is a tool.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which is the repository of the information and a guide to what it is, effectively. It does not contain, for example, the - it cannot - the actual physical items by which bodies were identified or the clothing or whatever it is. But it does contain a guide to how each of these victims was identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And it contains the documents as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if there's a statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- then the statement is there. It's -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Death certificates and all that, they're in there?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: At least I -- can I just say, I think so. I mean, I haven't personally looked at it myself. But I think that's how it's arranged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And this is a database containing all victims from 1992 to 1995 or 1996, if I understand it well?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It can -- unfortunately Ms. Pidwell's not here, because she's been dealing with it mainly. But my understanding is it contains all the victims connect -- we've extracted. It's a much bigger database, because it obviously contains Srebrenica and places like that. But it contains all the victims who have been identified as being killed from incidents which are reflected in our indictment, not -- as Mr. Zecevic says, not all of them are named in our -- our -- are named in our indictment, because subsequent information has come to light.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And just to make it clear, there are two differing strands to the Defence objection. The first is a legal one, namely, that we should not be allowed to lead evidence through the database of victims who are not named on our indictment. And that's a question of the various cases that have come before the Tribunal. And the second matter is this: That we shouldn't be allowed to use the database as the proof of death of anybody. That, in other words, we need to call the -- the experts who dealt with the exhumations, the evidence which shows that these bodies are, indeed, the bodies of people who were killed at the time. They're saying, as I understand Mr. Zecevic, Your Honours should not allow in the database as showing that all or any of these victims actually died. So that's -- no are the two strands. One is, are we allowed to call evidence through the database of all of the people or only those named. Secondly, is what's contained in the database sufficient proof. Or do we have to call each and every individual who found the bodies, identified them, and the method of identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, back -- still, before we go into the discussion, just the understanding. Is it right to say that - I could call it in the worst case scenario - OTP could provide the Trial Chamber and the Defence with the database, as such, database with 3.290 names and relating documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I mean -- at the worst case scenario, yes. Somebody could stand there going through it all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No, not standing there and going through it all. Tender it. Provide it to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The whole database?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As opposed to the hyperlinked schedules that you've got?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Well, we didn't get the hyperlinked schedules.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The Defence did. So I don't know -- I don't know how the hyperlinks schedules could perhaps resolve the problem of having the database or not having the database.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... hyperlinked. I won't -- when Your Honour Judge Delvoie asked for it, you didn't get the hyperlinked one, you just got the -- the schedules, the spreadsheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Perhaps with the hyperlinked ones it's enough, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I -- sorry, I now -- because we've got overlapping and I was distracted for a moment. Your Honours want the full database?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We are not ruling yet. But it's -- it's a possibility we're exploring, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Well, Your Honour, I don't want to say this off the top of my head. I would have to make inquiries of the person who's actually been dealing with it as to exactly what we could provide, if required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I may be of assistance, very briefly, Your Honours. The Annex B contains the names of the -- of the victims and some data and some -- some documents, ERN numbers. These documents have not been disclosed to us prior to filing of this, of these annexes, A and B, on the 22nd of July. After we reviewed, we asked that these particular ERN documents be disclosed to us. We were told that is the database. So we say, Yes, disclose to us the database but only for the victims which are listed in the schedules of the indictment. And that is the part of the legal argument that we presented to Your Honours. Now, when we received the -- the alleged underlying documents, the database, we found out that the database is nothing else but a number of other spreadsheets with no documents whatsoever, no death certificates, no -- no -- nothing of the sort. No decision of the Court of declaring the person dead -- the missing person dead or any kind of documentation, except on a -- on a very small basis. There are some documents. But if you -- if you -- if you would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... and what about the hyperlinks then? Is that a very small basis you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The hyperlinks actually connect one -- one -- one spreadsheet to the other spreadsheet to the other spreadsheet and the fourth spreadsheet. And there -- and the spreadsheet -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... and not to the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And there is -- well, that is precisely the problem, because there is no underlying documents, or we have not been disclosed the underlying documents. When we went to the meeting, we -- we -- we had a meeting with -- with the lady who is in charge of the -- of the database for the Office of the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Ms. Kipp.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... yes, Ms. Kipp. And we actually tried to find out the documents for one particular victim. We said, for example, number 112. And after 20 minutes it was -- she couldn't find it. So we say, Well, that is the -- that is it the -- that is the situation, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think it's appropriate. That was a -- a counsel to counsel meeting. Your Honour, that simple isn't right, because we've just turned it up, ourselves, and the autopsy reports are all there. We can see them. Now, Your Honours, the difficulty with all of this is that too many crooks, really, have been involved all together in this. But the simple answer is, if Your Honours want to understand the database, we can call Ms. Kipp who is the one who's really been dealing -- she wasn't the original person; that was an OTP investigator who no longer works. But she is familiar with the database and she can explain it exactly. But it's not right to say that no documents are in there and weren't hyperlinked. Now, it may be that there are links, if you like, to other databases, for example, where there have been declarations of death by the Sanski Most Court, because there are a number of associated databases. But, as I say, if Your Honours want to know exactly how this database is assembled, what it contains, and what is available, then it is really simpler for us to call Ms. Kipp than for everybody to start guessing and speculating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: One last question on this, as far as I'm concerned, Ms. Korner. You told us that you made the hyperlinks of the material you disclosed to the Defence and that took an eternity, right, to do?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It took a long time to do, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. You did that only for the victims in the indictment, or is it done for the other 1.806 as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, it's not. Because the only request we had was for the victims of the indictment -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... so if -- if the Court would ask you to provide the same thing but for all of the victims, that would take some time?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I can't tell you exactly how long, but I know it took -- I think it took the best part of three weeks to do that, yes, to do the ones that were named in the indictment. So we'd be talking about another month, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would like to apologise. I didn't want to disclose the contents of the counsel-to-counsel meeting. I just wanted to inform to the best of my abilities the Trial Chamber of what appears in our view to be the problem. Your Honours, we had listed six -- six parameters or six particular documents for each and ever victim, and we say: Okay, victim number 1, can we have these six documents, or at least three documents for that particular witness? What we received is another spreadsheet. When you click on the hyperlink, there is not a document that we asked for or any other document. What we get is another spreadsheet where this -- where this victim is -- is listed. And -- and when we -- when we ask what -- what is the meaning of this, they said, Well, this spreadsheet is the list of the victims as given by one of the sources. Now -- and that -- that is creating a problem. Because there might be the underlying document - I'm not saying - but we haven't seen it. We have not received the underlying document. When I say, Can I have the death certificate of that particular person, or the Court decision that the missing person has been declared dead, the specific person, that would be more than enough. But we never received any such document. Well, maybe some, but we haven't received the majority -- for the majority of the -- of the -- of the victims that we asked for. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- I think the problem has been - if I may say so with the greatest respect, and I have ever sympathy with Mr. Zecevic on this - is that they've not been using it properly. Because we've just pulled up -- we've just clicked on one and we've found the death certificate. So I think that Mr. Zecevic and myself, obviously, are not expert enough in the use of these databases. But it is possible to do it. There are documents in it. And, I mean, we literally have just clicked on one and pulled up a death certificate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But are you in the database now or are you on the spreadsheets?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We're on the hyperlinked -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Spreadsheets.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- spreadsheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's not the database.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Not the database.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Hyperlinked spreadsheet. So the -- it's been one of the problems. But it's -- as I say, it's Your Honours who've got to make the decision. And it's probably the simplest, and it shouldn't take very long, if we call Ms. Kipp, possibly putting Mr. Brown off, or whatever, and get her to explain this to you and show you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I wonder whether calling Mrs. Kipp just to let her explain how the database is -- functions and runs and what is supposed to be in it would be of some assistance but not entirely. Because what is basically needed are the underlying documents. Of course, if it is in the form of a database, which, as you said, is merely a tool to be -- to enable us to -- or to enable whoever to search in a more easy fashion than with a bunch of paper, but, still, it would seem to me that Defence and the Trial Chamber must have access to the documents, to the underlying documents, the source material.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So how can -- how could that eventually be arranged?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But they do. I mean, this is the point. The hyperlinking that we did, can I say it's not altogether sometimes the easiest, I accept, because there's an ERN range and it contains other documents, but they're all there. The hyperlinking. And, Your Honours, as I said, we can produce the documentation. I mean, we could actually, physically, I suppose, assemble a pile and do that. And that will take two months. And that would suffice, I think, for the non-computer-databased-literate people. But it's an enormous waste of effort. Your Honours, in no other case in this Tribunal has there ever been this kind of argument. And the reason is because it's accepted we have in this Tribunal the paperwork which these days is put onto electronically to show that these people are dead and that they died as a result of the crimes that were committed. If, however, Your Honours feel that the database and the tool that is there is not sufficient, then we will take whatever time it takes, physically assemble every piece of paper in a pile - for the -- I've forgotten how many victims it is now - and then Your Honours and Defence can go through them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Nobody is saying that, Ms. Korner. Not that I heard somebody say that. What we are saying is -- well, what I'm wondering now is, you say it -- it -- it works with the hyperlinks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's suppose it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But you have hyperlinked spreadsheets on 1.41 victims --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- and there -- it's not yet done for 1.806 victims. So that will take time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So my question is: Is it feasible that instead of doing this and providing us with -- with the spreadsheets, that you will provide us directly with the database? I don't know whether it's materially possible to -- to give the database to -- to the Court, or access to the database to the Court and to the Defence, but -- and if it's a good tool, if, of which I'm not yet sure, then you wouldn't have to -- to -- to do the hyperlink work which would take you a month.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Your Honours, can I discuss that? I don't -- I really am not up to speed enough on how this would be possible or what needs to be done. So I'd need to discuss it with -- well, certainly with Ms. Kipp, and possibly with Mr. Smith about what we can do about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It would -- it would perhaps be of assistance, Ms. Korner, if in the meantime we could have the spreadsheets you already provided to the Defence, the hyperlinked ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We can provide them to Your Honours as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. As we move towards the time when, for the usual technical reasons, we must rise, the -- item (i), the OTP motion of the 13th of December to reconsider denying protective measures to two witnesses, could we get an oral response from the Defence today?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can we consult over the break and inform the Trial Chamber immediately?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- are there matters to be dealt with following a break? Or are we at the end of --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Your Honours, I do have a couple which weren't on the agenda because it only came up yesterday. And they're short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But I wouldn't mind being able to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... well, I suppose it would be convenient to take a break now and resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the break I have been given an answer to Your Honours' question as to whether you or the Defence could be given access to the actual whole database. The answer to that is, No, very simply, because it's specific to the Office of the Prosecutor, the software, and it's linked with other matters. So the answer is, No, we can't do that. So the best we can hope to do is, if Your Honours would want us to do that, is to hyperlink the remainder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. Well, then -- then we would like to have, if possible, because it's -- it's ready, the hyperlinked spreadsheets today. Could that be done? Yes, for the 1400, of course -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... for the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Your Honour, yes. Yes, that can be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- for the ones in the indictment. And then we expect to be able to assess whether this is good material, for whatever better word, by Friday and that you know whether we need the -- the other ones to be hyperlinked as well. Does that work?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were there any other matters Your Honours wanted to raise, then? Because I need to come back to a couple of matters, as I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: No, you had indicated had you some matters to raise, so, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, the first is this. And I should really have mentioned it under "decisions needed on pending motions." Your Honours, we filed a motion on the 9th of this month seeking reconsideration of your oral ruling -- no, sorry, it's the one before that. Oh, yes, the admission of unsigned -- sorry. On 23rd of November - I'm so sorry - of your ruling on the admission of unsigned statements. And the reason we raised that is because we've either asked for permission to call an extra witness or to extend the testimony of Witness 023 -- I'm sorry, 228, to deal with that. So, again, if we could have that decision this week. Your Honour, the last matter is this. And it relates to the indictment. And I feel I ought to raise it at this stage. If Your Honours and the Defence go to Schedule B, the killings related to detention facilities, number 6 relates to the Koricanske Stijene massacre. And it says that it's in Skender Vakuf. Now, as technical points are being taken in this case, Your Honours may recall that the witness who was asked about it said that in fact the area of the killings was contained within the Travnik municipality rather than the Skender Vakuf. It was -- it was in the Serb-held part of that municipality. It's right to say that every adjudicated fact that we originally had over this municipality talks about Skender Vakuf. But that -- I do have to remind Your Honours that that is the -- the evidence that we've had, and whether either the Defence or Your Honours would require us to amend that description to reading something like, "in the vicinity of Skender Vakuf." As I say, it is a highly technical point, but I don't want to lose a particular incident because of a technical point. So I'm raising it at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is -- I'm not sure whether you are seeking leave to amend at this stage or whether you are inquiring of the other side whether they would take the -- to use your words, "technical objection," because, if it is the latter, I would have thought that when the objection is taken it would then provide the foundation for submissions. But, for myself, the -- I don't know that the Chamber would proprio motu require an amendment. But let me consult my brothers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Does the Defence have a response to this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that this is not only a technical issue. It is also an issue of responsibility and the jurisdiction over that area and who is responsible for that. This is something that we will be dealing in our final brief.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I don't think Mr. Krgovic has been listening to the evidence. It's quite clear that Banja Luka accepted jurisdiction over the investigation of this killing because they sent along the technicians and everybody like that. Your Honour, as I say, the killing are entirely related to detention facilities. And, of course, it's related to the fact that the men who were killed all came from Trnopolje. But it's right to say that there is some evidence, whether it's right or wrong we don't know, but it -- there's some evidence which hasn't been challenged --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: May I suggest, Ms. Korner, that having now had the benefit of what at least the Defence of Zupljanin would say, that you should advise yourself as to whether the prudent course would be for you to make a formal application for amendment of the indictment in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, then, can I do that right now, Your Honour. It seems to be the simplest and we can get it out of the way. Can I apply to amend item 6, the killings at the Vlasic Mountain, to read "in or in the vicinity of the -- Skender Vakuf."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, before you take the floor, could I just be sure about what exactly it is Ms. Korner is suggesting. On page 21 of the indictment, which is Schedule B, killings related to detention facilities, there's a heading which is called 6. That indicates Skender Vakuf. And then there's an explanation in the next column, which is labelled 6.1, and that reads: "The execution of a large number of men from Trnopolje camp at the Vlasic mountain." Now, where is it that Ms. Korner wants to have the amendment? Is that in the heading, under 6, or is it the subheading, under 6.1? Or both?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... Your Honour, it says: The execution of a large number of men from Trnopolje camp at the Vlasic mountain. That's correct. Vlasic mountain is the English translation of Koricanske Stijene ... more or less. I heard somebody yell "no," so I thought I better add "more or less."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I'm asking for the amendment to where it says: "6, Skender Vakuf."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And could you repeat to us, again, the amendment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "In or in the vicinity of Skender Vakuf."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Ms. Korner, to add to the confusion, I'm afraid, I noticed that in your -- in the spreadsheet A, exhumations, the victims are listed by municipality. Yes? And incident number 6.1. Is, indeed, Skender Vakuf; but the header says "municipality of exhumation." Is that -- is that right? I mean, it -- it -- it doesn't seem right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know that it can be because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It doesn't seem right. Because in the -- in the -- in the -- there is another -- another indication that for 200 out of 295 victims under -- under 6.1, the whereabouts are unknown. Which seems to indicate that there is no exhumation site.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: My recollection is, and I believe the witness dealt with it, is that the bodies have not yet been exhumed. Because you mentioned there is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... okay. So for the general -- for the Annex A exhumation spreadsheet where it said in the first column, column A, "municipality of exhumation is ..." shall I take that to be incorrect? Do you take, for instance --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You have listed -- the -- the victims are listed in different worksheets in the spreadsheet by municipality. You have Banja Luka, Bileca, and whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And that's normally - normally - the municipality you find under A but under the header "municipality of exhumation," which --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I -- can I say, I think I need, again, and I'm sorry, to make some inquiries about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If it is meant to be -- I think it's meant to be the municipality of -- of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- of the incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Of the incident. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah. Then --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm afraid I really will have to go back over that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Then I just mention another slight problem. Within this incident there are, I think, four victims listed as being from Prijedor or ... in the Column A.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Column A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Municipality of exhumation, well, to see that, you need -- you need to put together the Prijedor worksheet and the -- and the Skender Vakuf worksheet. Or you can look to both worksheets and see that in each of them you have listed incidents 6.1, which if the incident happened in Skender Vakuf, it can't happen in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. No. I mean, it's a question. Your Honours are quite right. And I will make some inquiries and try and sort that one out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And same goes perhaps for Banja Luka. I -- I think I know that Banja Luka and Sanski Most are two different municipalities, if I'm not wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour is quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Under Banja Luka there are some 20 entries "Sanski Most."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But it's for the same incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, can I say, I'll get back to you on that one as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So is the position that you're withdrawing your oral motion with a view to returning after you would have had an opportunity to look at this --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. That's a separate matter as to how -- that's got nothing do with what the indictment says. The indictment says: "Place, Skender Vakuf." As I say, it is so mind-bogglingly technical and so little to do with the actual proof of case. But it is a fact. And as I say, if Your Honours, as a result of Mr. Krgovic's intervention --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Okay. I just wanted to be clear with having regard to the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... no, I think it still should because it -- it -- there is now an argument as to whether the actual site of the killing, which is what this is meant to represent, was Travnik or Skender Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So could we hear the Defence on the application to amend made by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours we were not put on notice that this is going to be on the -- on -- one of the issues on the agenda for today's Status Conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, as Ms. Korner has indicated, whereas this is a motion without notice, it is, on the face of it, fairly straightforward and something which counsel could not unreasonably be invited to respond on -- on -- in -- to immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I -- I understand, Your Honours. But I didn't have time to consult with the -- either Mr. Krgovic or the members my team. If you would give us a couple minutes, we will be able to -- to give an answer to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... that's quite right because it was only yesterday when I was actually going through the indictment as a precursor to this Status Conference that I was reminded that that had been the evidence. And so I didn't bother to add it to the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You say "a couple of minutes," Mr. Zecevic. Is it necessary for us to rise, or is this a matter you can sort out sotto voce?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We can consult in the courtroom, I guess, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I consulted with Mr. Krgovic, and I will leave the floor to him to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in general, we don't have anything against this amendment sought by the OTP. But I think that what they just said was not precise enough when it comes to the site of executions or killings. I think they would need to give the details about the municipality and the exact site, in order to avoid any uncertainties about the area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, the fact is that through, I would think now, half a dozen cases, if not more, the Koricanske Stijene killings have been listed as occurring in the municipality of Skender Vakuf.
